SDMs: daily exercises

Clarke van Steenderen

2025-05-06

Species Distribution Modelling: R proficiency exercises

Below are daily R exercises for you to complete. We will go over these together after you have tried them yourself. Part of our daily class discussion will involve issues you encountered with these exercises. Use the package help files to find out which parameters are needed. If you use AI such as ChatGPT to help you code, make sure that you understand what it’s doing, and that you have a very good grasp of the fundamentals.

Set up, and ggplot specs

This is just to make sure that you have all the necessary libraries installed, and that your ggplots look nice.

# create folders in your working directory in which to store data and figures as you proceed. The !dir.exists ensures that the folder isn't overwritten if it exists already

if (!dir.exists("data")) dir.create("data")
if (!dir.exists("figures")) dir.create("figures")

pacman::p_load(
  NicheMapR, magrittr, dplyr, tidyr, janitor, raster, sp, ggplot2, rgbif, dismo,
  ENMeval, sf, readr, terra, geodata, rnaturalearth, corrplot, gtools, igraph, usdm,
  factoextra, gridExtra, ecospat, forcats
)

# Change ggplot theme
theme_set(
  theme_classic() +
    theme(
      panel.border = element_rect(colour = "black", fill = NA),
      axis.text = element_text(colour = "black"),
      axis.title.x = element_text(margin = unit(c(2, 0, 0, 0), "mm")),
      axis.title.y = element_text(margin = unit(c(0, 4, 0, 0), "mm")),
      legend.position = "none"
    )
)

# Set the theme for the maps
theme_opts = list(
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = 'white', colour = NA),
    plot.background = element_rect(),
    axis.line = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(colour = "black"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(colour = "black"),
    axis.ticks = element_line(colour = "black"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(colour = "black"),
    axis.title.y = element_text(colour = "black"),
    plot.title = element_text(colour = "black"),
    panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA),
    legend.key = element_blank()
  )
)

Week 1

Exercise 1

Use the geodata::sp_occurrence() function to download all the available records for the endangered Brenton Blue butterfly, Orachrysops niobe, from the GBIF database.

  • Do a quick count of how many occurrences there were for each country in the country column. Hint: use dplyr::count()
  • Do another count, but this time for the occurrences in each province in the adm1 column
  • In the adm1 column for province, replace all NAs with “unknown”
  • Create a bar plot using ggplot2, where you show the total record counts per province. Set the y-axis range from 0 to 45, with intervals of 5. Colour the bars any colour you like, and give them a black border (use fill = "your_colour", colour = "black") to do this
  • See if you can order the bars from largest to smallest, using the fct_infreq() function in the forcats library
  • Create a new data frame, where you keep only the species, lat, and lon columns
  • Remove all duplicate GPS records from this data frame
  • Using nrow(), print out the number of rows in the original download and in the cleaned version (after duplicates were removed)
  • Save the final data frame as both an RDS and CSV file

Some starting code is provided to get you going:

# Download all available records from GBIF
or.niobe = geodata::sp_occurrence(
  genus = "Orachrysops",
  species = "niobe",
  download = TRUE,
  geo = TRUE,
  removeZeros = TRUE
)

# count records per country
# create a bar plot
# Select the specified columns
# Remove duplicate GPS records

# save as an RDS file
saveRDS(object = or.niobe_final, file = "data/or.niobe.rds")

# save as a CSV

Exercise 2

Read in your saved RDS data frame saved in Exercise 1, and:

  • Plot all the records for Orachrysops niobe onto a map of South Africa (use rnaturalearth::ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") %>% dplyr::filter(name %in% c("South Africa")))
  • Colour the GPS points dark red
  • Crop the map to exclude Marion Island (use coord_sf(crs = 4326, xlim = c(16, 33), ylim = c(-35, -22), expand = FALSE) to set the x and y limits)
  • Give the map an appropriate title (ggtitle("title_here"))
  • Try to add in a North arrow (ggspatial::annotation_north_arrow()) and scale bar to the map (ggspatial::annotation_scale()
  • Save the map as an RDS file, and a PNG image (5 x 5, dpi = 350)

Your ggplot function should follow this template:

# get South Africa raster map
southafrica_ext = rnaturalearth::ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") %>%
                  dplyr::filter(name %in% c("South Africa"))

# Plot GPS points on SA map
YOUR_MAP = ggplot() +
  # Add raster layer of SA map 
  geom_sf(data = southafrica_ext, alpha = 0.5, fill = "grey80") +
  # Add your GPS points 
  geom_point(
    data = YOUR_DATA, 
    size = YOUR_SIZE,
    colour = "YOUR_COLOUR",
    aes(x = lon, y = lat)
  )  +
  # Set SA CRS, and crop
  coord_sf(
    crs = 4326,
    xlim = c(16, 33),      
    ylim = c(-35, -22),
    expand = FALSE
  ) + 
  xlab("Longitude") + 
  ylab("Latitude") +
  ggtitle("YOUR_TITLE") +
  # ADD SCALE BAR
  # ADD NORTH ARROW
  )

Your map should look something like the one below. You will notice that Lesotho and Eswatini/Swaziland are coloured white, and therefore excluded. Try to include these in another version of the map. Hint: Eswatini needs to be referred to as "eSwatini" when you select country names in the rnaturalearth::ne_countries() function.

Exercise 3

The command provincial_borders = ne_states(country = "South Africa", returnclass = "sf") provides South African provincial boundaries. See if you can add these to your ggplot map from Exercise 2.

  • Now colour the provinces, so that the Western Cape Province is lightgreen. To colour individual provinces, you will need to use aes(fill = name), such that: geom_sf(data = provincial_borders, color = "black", aes(fill = name)), followed by scale_fill_manual(), where you need to supply a colour to each province. E.g. scale_fill_manual(values = c(Northern Cape = "grey80, ....))
  • Save the map as a 5 x 5 PNG image with a dpi of 350, AND as an RDS file.

Some tips are given below:

southafrica_ext = rnaturalearth::ne_countries(scale = "medium",
                  returnclass = "sf") %>%
                  dplyr::filter(name %in% c("South Africa"))

# provincial borders
provincial_borders = rnaturalearth::ne_states(country = "South Africa", returnclass = "sf")

YOUR_MAP = ggplot() +
  # Add raster layer of SA map 
  geom_sf(data = southafrica_ext, alpha = 0.5, fill = "grey80") +
  # Add provincial borders
  geom_sf(data = provincial_borders, color = "black", aes(fill = name)) +
  # Colour provinces individually
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Northern Cape" = "grey80",
      "KwaZulu-Natal" = "grey80",
      "Free State" = "grey80",
      "Eastern Cape" = "grey80",
      "Limpopo" = "grey80",
      "North West" = "grey80",
      "Mpumalanga" = "grey80",
      "Western Cape" = "grey80",
      "Gauteng" = "grey80"
    ),
    name = "Province"
  ) +
  # Add your GPS points 
  # Add the rest of the plotting parameters, as before
  
  # Save as an RDS and PNG

Create your own function

So far, you have encountered numerous R functions to process your data, run statistical tests, create graphics, etc. You can create your own functions quite easily, if you have repetitive code that you need to re-run with different inputs. Below is an example of how you would structure a function in R that produces a simple box plot given a series of values and a grouping variable (here, we’ll create 100 random positive numbers, and randomly assign A, B, or C to each value as a grouping variable).

# Create your function
myboxplot = function(DF, value_col, group_col, fill.col = "lightpink") {
  
 plot = ggplot(DF, aes(x = .data[[group_col]], y = .data[[value_col]], fill = .data[[group_col]])) +
  geom_boxplot(color = "black", fill = fill.col) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = group_col, y = value_col, title = "My Boxplot Function")
 
 return(plot)
}

# Create some example data -> randomly create 100 values, and randomly assign
# A, B, or C to each
df = data.frame(
  value = abs(rnorm(100)),
  group = sample(c("A", "B", "C"), 100, replace = TRUE)
)

head(df)
##        value group
## 1 0.46106535     A
## 2 0.39725279     B
## 3 1.14557741     C
## 4 1.22912015     B
## 5 0.01799302     C
## 6 1.33612735     B
# Call your function
myboxplot(df, value_col = "value", group_col = "group", fill.col = "royalblue")

Over to you:

  • Adapt the myboxplot function above to allow the user to (1) specify the alpha value for colouring the plot, and (2) edit the axis labels and plot title
  • Now, create your own new function that plots a map of South Africa. This function should take in three parameters: (1) a data frame that contains lat and lon GPS points, (2) the name of the column containing the latitude values, and (3) the name of the column containing the longitude values. Use the code below that we used previously as a framework. If you want to, you can also add the colour of the points as an additional parameter, and the ability to change the point size, shape, position of the North arrow and scale bar, etc.
mySAmap = function(PARAMETER1, PARAMETER2, PARAMETER3){
  
southafrica_ext = rnaturalearth::ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") %>%
                  dplyr::filter(name %in% c("South Africa"))

map = ggplot() +
  # Add raster layer of SA map 
  geom_sf(data = southafrica_ext, alpha = 0.5, fill = "grey80") +
  # Add GPS points 
  geom_point(
    data = PARAMETER, 
    size = 1.5,
    colour = "darkred",
    aes(x = .data[[PARAMETER]], y = .data[[PARAMETER]])
  )  +
  # Set CRS 
  coord_sf(
    crs = 4326,
    xlim = c(16, 33),      
    ylim = c(-35, -22),
    expand = FALSE
  ) + 
  xlab("Longitude") + 
  ylab("Latitude") +
  ggspatial::annotation_scale(
    location = "br",          # 'bl' = bottom left
    style = "ticks",
    width_hint = 0.2
  ) +
  # Add north arrow
  ggspatial::annotation_north_arrow(
    location = "br",
    which_north = "true",
    pad_x = unit(0.175, "in"),
    pad_y = unit(0.3, "in"),
    style = ggspatial::north_arrow_fancy_orienteering
  ) +
  theme_classic()

return(map)

} #mySAmap function

# now test the function on any of the data sets we downloaded from GBIF in earlier exercises

Exercise 6

This activity will teach you a little more about lists in R. A list is a container which can hold one or more objects. Perhaps you have two data frames containing GBIF information, you can pack them both into a single list. Below is a simple example of how you can combine objects into a list. Here, we’ll create three data frames containing five random numbers between 1 and 100, and then store them in a list called mylist. We’ll call the first item in the list, DF1, spA, the second, DF2, spB, and the last spC. Once created, you can refer to your individual data frames using the $ sign; for example mylist$spA. If you want to later combine all the objects in your list into a single data frame, you can run dplyr::bind_rows(mylist, .id = "source"), where .id = "source" ensures that an additional grouping column is included to tell you which object (here spA, spB, spC) each value came from.

# create random data frames
DF1 = data.frame(values = sample(1:100, 5))
DF2 = data.frame(values = sample(1:100, 5))
DF3 = data.frame(values = sample(1:100, 5))

# shuttle them into a list
mylist = list(spA = DF1, spB = DF2, spC = DF3)

# refer to the individual objects like this:
mylist$spA
##   values
## 1      9
## 2     70
## 3     52
## 4      5
## 5     89
mylist$spB
##   values
## 1     59
## 2     55
## 3     12
## 4     49
## 5     47
mylist$spC
##   values
## 1     39
## 2      5
## 3     78
## 4     12
## 5     36
# if you want to combine all objects in the list into one DF, you can run:
combo_df = dplyr::bind_rows(mylist, .id = "source")

What we can do now is loop through each item in our mylist list, and perform some kind of check or operation. For example, we can sum the values in each sp object in our list, and print the result to the screen. for-loops take the following format:

for(item in container){
  # run some code
  # access an item by referencing its position in the list:
  container[[item]]
}

In our example (k can be anything you want; i, item, etc. It simply acts as a counter that starts at 1 and ends at the size of the list; here that would mean that it runs from 1 to 3, since we had 3 items in our list):

for(k in 1:length(mylist)){
  print( sum(mylist[[k]]) )
}
## [1] 225
## [1] 222
## [1] 170
# if you want to add some descriptive output text:
for(k in 1:length(mylist)){
  print(paste0("The sum of ", names(mylist[k]), " is: ", sum(mylist[[k]]) ) )
}
## [1] "The sum of spA is: 225"
## [1] "The sum of spB is: 222"
## [1] "The sum of spC is: 170"

There is an even shorter way of running a loop, using sapply:

sapply(mylist, sum, USE.NAMES = TRUE)
## spA spB spC 
## 225 222 170

# run the loop

As a final exercise for this section:

  • Combine the three objects in bitis.list into one data frame, and call this combo_bitis
  • Modify the function you created in the previous exercise (mySAmap()) to accept an additional parameter for a grouping column. Call this function mySAmap.groups
  • Plot a map of South Africa with the GPS coordinates of the three adder species, where you colour each species differently using default colours. If you want to add a different palette of default colours, try adding something like scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") to your ggplot. Google some other palette sets that you could use
  • Run your function a second time, but this time around filter the GPS coordinates so that you remove the points in Namibia. You can use dplyr::filter(combo_bitis, country == "South Africa"). If you want to keep Lesotho and eSwatini as well, you can use: dplyr::filter(combo_bitis, country %in% c("South Africa", "Lesotho", "Swaziland", "eSwatini"))
  • If you want to edit the legend title and names of groups, you can add this to your final plot:
scale_color_brewer(
  palette = "Set1",
  name = "Species",
  labels = c(
    "b.albanica" = "B. albanica",

)

# OR

scale_color_discrete(
  name = "Species",

    "b.albanica" = "B. albanica",
    "b.atropos"  = "B. atropos",
    "b.cornuta"  = "B. cornuta"

)

  ) +

Exercise 4

Using your Bradypodion occidentale GPS file, create a new column that contains only the year from the column called eventDate. I.e. 2025-01-13T07:30:14 should become 2025. To do this, use the base R substr() function, where you provide the number of characters you want to retain. For example: substr("Bradypodion", 1, 4) will extract characters 1 to 4 from the word “Bradypodion”, returning “Brad”.

  • Once you have this new data column of years only, create a data frame with the total counts for each year. Remove any NAs, and create a line plot using ggplot, where you show the total number of GBIF records for each year (this should be from the year 1933 to the present)
  • Colour the line lightblue, set its width to lwd = 1.5, and alpha = 0.5
  • Set the y-axis to intervals of 5, and the limit from 0 to 35. You can add this to your ggplot to achieve this: scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 35, by = 5), limits = c(0, 35)).

Your graph should resemble:

Create a function

Create a dynamic function that automates the creation of the plot above. This function should read in a data frame that has been downloaded from GBIF, extract the year that each entry was recorded, tally up the counts for each year, and plot a line chart. Your function should include parameters for the following:

  • line colour
  • line thickness
  • point size
  • point shape
  • angle of the x-axis labels
  • the y min and y max values, and the y-interval

As a reminder, use the template below for building functions (the parameter names can be changed, these are just suggestions). It’s good practice to set default values where applicable, to avoid errors if the user doesn’t provide a value.

plot.recs = function(data, line.col, line.w, pt.size, pt.shape, x.angle, ymin, ymax, breaks){
  
  data$shortdate = substr(data[[eventdate.col]], 1, 4)
  
  YOURPLOT = ggplot() +
  # your plotting code
    
  return(YOURPLOT)
}

Now, as a final touch to your function, add an error message if the user provides a column name that does not exist in the data frame they provide. Below is some pseudo-code to get you started. Remember that negations in R are denoted with an exclamation mark (!), and if you want to check whether one thing exists in another, you can use %in%.

if (EVENTDATECOLUMN is not in the names(INPUTDATA)) {
    stop(paste0("Column ", EVENTDATECOLUMN, " not found in the data frame."))
  }
